subtype: Stage 1: Task feels big or dull [Actor]
passage:
After-school club note, Sudha (carer), Wednesday
Tanvir, 9, opened his solar system project folder at 4:10. He looked at the blank chart paper and the list of eight planets, sighed and said, "This is soooo long." He sharpened a pencil that was already sharp. Then he asked for his snack early. By 4:25 he was building a tower with the reading-corner blocks, humming, much happier.
When I asked about the project, he said, "Later. It's boring and I don't know where to start."
What I did next: I sat beside him and asked him to draw just the sun, nothing else. He finished it in five minutes and asked if he could do Mercury too.

qa.q: What did Tanvir build at 4:25?
qa.a: A tower with the reading-corner blocks.

qa.q: Why did Tanvir sharpen an already sharp pencil and ask for his snack early?
qa.a: Looking at the big project made him feel bored and a little dread, so he wanted quick relief by doing something easier.

qa.q: Why did Sudha's idea of drawing just the sun work?
qa.a: It made the big project small and clear, so starting felt easy, and once he had started he wanted to keep going.

qa.q: How might Sudha see Tanvir's move from the project to the blocks?
qa.a: Sudha seems to understand the dodge rather than feel annoyed, hearing 'I don't know where to start' as the real problem.

grounding: Shows a child feeling dread and boredom at a big project and drifting to a snack and blocks for quick relief.

subtype: Stage 1: Task feels big or dull [Actor]
passage:
Dear Diary,
Today Ma'am gave us an essay, My Favourite Festival, one full page. When I opened my notebook after school my tummy went heavy. A WHOLE page.
So I got up for water. Then I ate two biscuits. Then I just checked one level of my car game on Papa's old phone. Then one more level.
Gurleen didi came and said, "Kishore, you've been 'starting' for one hour."
I said I was thinking. I wasn't really thinking. I just didn't want the heavy feeling.
Now it's 8 pm and I still have zero lines. And the heavy feeling is bigger.
Kishore

qa.q: How many biscuits did Kishore eat?
qa.a: Two biscuits.

qa.q: What did Kishore feel on opening the notebook, and what did Kishore want instead?
qa.a: Kishore's tummy went heavy at the thought of a whole page, and Kishore wanted to escape that feeling with water, biscuits and the car game.

qa.q: What small step could help Kishore start the essay?
qa.a: Kishore could write just the festival's name and one line about it, so the page feels smaller, before the game comes out 🙂.

qa.q: What might Gurleen didi notice about Kishore's 'thinking'?
qa.a: Gurleen didi sees an hour of 'starting' with no writing, and may guess that the essay feels too big rather than that Kishore is lazy.

grounding: Illustrates a child's heavy feeling at a whole-page essay and the pull toward water, biscuits and a game for relief.

subtype: Stage 1: Task feels big or dull [Actor]
passage:
Tutor's note for home, Wednesday
Irfan opened his science project folder today at 4:30. He looked at the empty chart paper and sighed a big sigh. Then he asked for water. Then he wanted to sharpen all his pencils. Then he asked if he could have a snack first. By 4:50 he had not written a word.
I don't think he is being naughty. He seemed a bit overwhelmed, maybe bored by how big the chart looked. Looking at it made him want something easier, straight away.
So we made the first step tiny: write just the title. He did it in two minutes and looked pleased. Tomorrow we'll do one box.
Farida, tutor

qa.q: What did Irfan want to sharpen?
qa.a: All his pencils.

qa.q: What was Irfan feeling as he looked at the empty chart paper?
qa.a: He felt a little overwhelmed and bored, which made him want something easier straight away.

qa.q: Why did making the first step tiny help?
qa.a: Writing just the title felt easy, so Irfan could start without the dread of the whole project.

qa.q: How might Irfan's parents feel reading this note?
qa.a: They may feel relieved that Farida sees it as overwhelm rather than naughtiness, and hopeful about the tiny steps.

grounding: Shows a tutor's note on a child who looks at a big project, feels a small wave of dread or boredom, and turns to easier things.

Dear diary,
I had to start my Hindi essay today. It's about "My Favourite Festival." I sat at my desk and looked at the empty page for a long time. It felt so long and boring. My tummy felt a bit funny.
So I went to get a biscuit. Then I played one game on Sunaina didi's phone. Just one. Then I watched the birds on the window. Then Mumma called for dinner.
The page is still empty. I feel a bit bad now.
Tomorrow I'll do it. Maybe.
Gopika

qa.a: "My Favourite Festival."

qa.q: What was Gopika feeling while looking at the empty page?
qa.a: Gopika felt bored and a little uneasy, with a funny tummy, and wanted something easier.

qa.q: What small step could help Gopika start tomorrow?
qa.a: Writing just the first sentence, like the name of the festival, before any biscuit or game.

qa.q: What might Sunaina didi think if she saw the empty page?
qa.a: Sunaina didi might feel amused or a little concerned, knowing her phone was part of the escape.

grounding: Shows a child's diary about looking at an essay, feeling bored and uneasy, and turning to a biscuit, a game and the birds.

subtype: Stage 1: Task feels big or dull [Actor]
passage:
In the village near Belgaum, Suraj sat on the verandah with his maths workbook open. Twenty sums for tomorrow. He looked at the first one and felt his shoulders droop. So many. So boring.
"Amma, can I have a guava?"
"Finish your sums first," said Manjula from the kitchen.
"Just one guava!"
He ate it slowly. Then he watched the neighbour's goat. Then he chased a lizard with his pencil. The sums waited.
Manjula came out and saw the empty page. She sat down beside him. "Twenty is a lot. Let's just do the first two together."
Suraj groaned, but picked up his pencil.

qa.q: How many sums did Suraj have?
qa.a: Twenty sums.

qa.q: What was Suraj feeling when his shoulders drooped?
qa.a: He felt bored and a bit dreadful at how many sums there were, so he looked for relief.

qa.q: Which of Manjula's choices helped, and why?
qa.a: Sitting beside Suraj and suggesting just the first two sums, which made the start feel small.

qa.q: What might Manjula be thinking when she sees the empty page?
qa.a: Manjula may feel a little frustrated but understanding, seeing that the task felt too big.

grounding: Shows a child facing a page of sums, feeling boredom and dread, and turning to a guava, a goat and a lizard.

subtype: Stage 1: Task feels big or dull [Actor]
passage: Freya put the blank poster board on the kitchen table in Glasgow and stared at it. "Volcanoes," the teacher's sheet said. "Include a diagram, three facts and a picture." It looked enormous. Her tummy did a small flip, the same one she got before swimming lessons. She picked up a pencil, drew half a triangle, and stopped. Maybe she needed a snack first. She got a biscuit. Then she noticed her cousin Priscila's comic lying on the sofa and read two pages, just to see what happened. Then the cat wanted stroking. When Mum called from upstairs, "How's the volcano going?", Freya looked at the half triangle and felt the flip again.

qa.q: What did the teacher's sheet ask Freya to include?
qa.a: A diagram, three facts and a picture.

qa.q: What was Freya feeling when she stared at the blank poster board?
qa.a: She felt a small wave of dread, a tummy flip like before swimming lessons, because the task looked enormous.

qa.q: What small step could help Freya start?
qa.a: Finishing just the triangle diagram, or writing one fact, would make the big poster feel smaller.

qa.q: What might Mum be picturing when she asks about the volcano?
qa.a: Mum may imagine Freya busy working, not knowing she has drifted to a biscuit, a comic and the cat.

grounding: Shows a child facing a big project, feeling a small wave of dread and drifting to easier things like a snack and a comic.
